Over five years, sales grew about 11% a year, but profit about 55% a year, as copper prices climbed. It earns about ₹24 a year on every hundred rupees invested, and has no debt. The share closed at ₹419, well below its one-year high of ₹760.
investing.why: Its fortunes follow the world copper price, which hit record highs this year, so profit nearly tripled last quarter. In August the government sold about 6% of the company through an offer for sale to raise money, cutting its stake to about 60%.
investing.soWhat: Today you pay about ₹26 for each rupee of yearly profit (its P/E). Over five years, buyers usually paid about ₹53.
investing.take: A debt-free way to own India's copper, if metal prices hold up.
investing.watch: The world copper price, and any further government share sale.

terms.meaning: Price paid for each rupee of yearly profit

tech.label: Tech · 21 Nov 2026
tech.headline: Signal blocks screenshots to keep phone AI assistants out of chats
tech.summary: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, now blocks screenshots by default on iPhones running iOS 27. On Android, it switches on its 'Screen security' setting when it spots an AI assistant trying to read the screen. This is live now, announced on Friday. Signal says built-in helpers like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence read whatever is on screen, pulling private chats out of the app.
tech.why: Encryption only protects messages while they travel. Once words appear on your display, any helper that 'sees' it can copy them elsewhere. Signal did the same to Microsoft's Recall on Windows last year. It admits the fix is incomplete and cannot yet work on Macs.
tech.soWhat: If you screenshot chats as proof of payments or plans, expect a block. Switching it off exposes your contacts' messages to AI too.
tech.take: Phone makers should give apps a simple off-switch for AI snooping.
tech.watch: Apple and Google answering Signal's demand for an AI opt-out switch.
tech.tryThis: On iPhone, open Signal Settings and check that 'Block Siri AI' is on. On a Mac, add Signal to Excluded Apps under System Settings, then Siri.

terms.meaning: Scrambled so only sender and receiver can read
Software helper that reads and acts on your behalf

tech.headline: Google's Gemini can now click through your Mac apps for you
tech.summary: Google's Gemini app for Mac can now operate other apps and websites for you. Describe a chore, such as filling a shipping form using details from a PDF, and Gemini clicks, types and fills it in a separate background window while you keep working. It began rolling out on Thursday, 19 November, but only in English in the US, for paid Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers.
tech.why: This is called 'computer use': instead of only giving advice, the AI acts. Rivals want the same job. TechCrunch, citing a job posting and Bloomberg, reports Apple is building its own agent that runs Macs, though that work remains early.
tech.soWhat: Not available in India yet. When it arrives, it could save hours of repetitive office clicking, if you limit which apps it touches.
tech.take: Agents that do chores are useful; approving every key step should stay mandatory.
tech.watch: When Google expands Mac computer use beyond the US and English.
tech.tryThis: List the apps on your laptop that hold bank, health or work secrets, so you know which ones never to grant an AI agent.

tech.label: Tech · 21 Nov 2026
tech.headline: UN talks on AI-run 'killer robot' weapons run into overtime
tech.summary: Countries meeting at the UN in Geneva missed Friday's deadline to decide whether to start negotiating rules for weapons that pick and attack targets on their own. Talks among the 128 nations in the treaty ran past midnight into Saturday. A draft seen by Reuters does not commit to legally binding rules right away, even though about 100 states support them. Nothing is agreed yet.
tech.why: Such LAWS are already real: AI-assisted weapons have been used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East. Every member must agree for a decision to pass, so a few holdouts can stall it. The US, Russia and Israel oppose binding limits; Russia slowed this week's process.
tech.soWhat: Without binding rules, armies everywhere, including in India's neighbourhood, can deploy AI weapons with no agreed limits on human control.
tech.take: A non-binding deal after over a decade of talks would be a failure.
tech.watch: The final Geneva text and any mandate for formal treaty negotiations.
tech.tryThis: Search for the Stop Killer Robots coalition and read its short explainer on what human control over weapons should mean.

terms.meaning: Lethal autonomous weapons: they select and attack targets themselves
Countries must obey it, not just aim for it

tech.headline: Sarvam defends running Chinese AI models on its Indian servers
tech.summary: Bengaluru's Sarvam AI opened Token Factory to everyone on 16 November. It is a paid service that lets businesses run AI models on Sarvam's computers in India through one connection. Alongside its own Sarvam 105B, it offers Chinese models such as DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM. Critics asked why a company backed under the IndiaAI Mission sells access to Chinese AI. Sarvam says it uses privately bought chips.
tech.why: The government picked Sarvam to build homegrown models and gave it subsidised computing for training, which the company says ended in March 2026. Hosting a foreign model locally keeps data here, but does not make the model Indian. Other firms, like E2E Networks, offer similar services.
tech.soWhat: Indian firms can now pay in rupees for strong AI kept on Indian soil, but should still check data and retention rules.
tech.take: Selling Chinese models is fine business; it just isn't sovereign AI.
tech.watch: Any IndiaAI Mission guidance on what subsidised model-builders may also sell.
tech.tryThis: Before your company sends data to any AI service, ask where it runs and whether prompts are stored; Sarvam offers no-storage on request.

psychology.label: Psychology · 21 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Rewarding children for something they love can make them love it less
psychology.summary: Your child loves drawing. Should you pay them a sticker for every picture? In a 1973 test at a Stanford nursery school, 51 children aged three to five drew with markers. Some were promised a gold-seal 'Good Player Award' first. A week or two later, during free play, those children spent about 8.6% of their time drawing, roughly half as much as the others.
psychology.why: Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett called it the overjustification effect. Children who drew for a promised prize seemed to decide they drew for the prize. A surprise certificate, given afterwards, did no harm. The promised group's pictures were also rated lower in quality.
psychology.soWhat: Marks, star charts and cash for reading can quietly turn a hobby your child enjoys into a chore.
psychology.take: Praise effort after the fact; never put a price on curiosity.
psychology.watch: Notice whether a rewarded activity drops off once the reward stops coming.

terms.meaning: Expected rewards shrinking our own interest in something

sources.label: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

study.authors: Mark R. Lepper, David Greene and Richard E. Nisbett

psychology.example: A boy who read comics for fun stops reading once his parents start paying ten rupees a book.
psychology.useThisWeek: Replace one promised reward with a surprise thank-you after the task is done.

psychology.label: Psychology · 21 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: A shaky bridge can make a stranger seem more attractive
psychology.summary: Ever felt a spark with someone after a scary film or a bumpy ride? In 1974, a woman stopped 85 men in Canada on one of two bridges: a swaying one 230 feet above rocks, or a steady one 10 feet up. She gave out her number. Nine of 18 men from the scary bridge called her, against two of 16 from the steady one.
psychology.why: Psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron called it misattribution of arousal. A racing heart from fear can be mistaken for attraction to whoever is nearby. The authors noted limits: thrill-seekers may choose the scary bridge, and the sample was small and all male.
psychology.soWhat: Nerves before an interview or a match can tint how you judge the people around you.
psychology.take: Big feelings in tense moments deserve a second look once you calm down.
psychology.watch: Check your heart rate next time a decision feels exciting rather than right.

terms.meaning: Blaming a bodily feeling on the wrong cause

sources.label: Dutton and Aron (1974), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

study.authors: Donald G. Dutton and Arthur P. Aron

psychology.example: After a thrilling Giant Wheel ride at a mela, your companion suddenly seems more charming.
psychology.useThisWeek: Before replying to a heated message, take ten slow breaths, then decide.

psychology.label: Psychology · 21 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: After a chat, people like you more than you think
psychology.summary: You leave a party replaying every awkward pause. Did they find you boring? In a 2018 study, 36 strangers chatted for five minutes in a Yale lab, then rated each other. On a seven-point scale, people liked their partner about 5.8 but guessed their partner liked them only about 5.2. Everyone underrated themselves.
psychology.why: Erica Boothby and colleagues named this the liking gap. People focus on their own stumbles and miss warm signals like smiles. Across five studies with 442 people, the gap held, even for college roommates over several months. Most participants were American students or workshop attendees.
psychology.soWhat: That new colleague or neighbour probably enjoyed meeting you. Fear of a bad impression is often wrong.
psychology.take: Assume you went over better than it felt, and follow up.
psychology.watch: After your next first meeting, guess their rating, then ask a friend.

terms.meaning: Underestimating how much others like us

sources.label: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark (2018), Psychological Science

study.authors: Erica J. Boothby, Gus Cooney, Gillian M. Sandstrom and Margaret S. Clark

psychology.example: You skip messaging a new teammate after lunch because you think you talked too much.
psychology.useThisWeek: Send one 'nice meeting you' message to someone you met recently.

psychology.label: Psychology · 21 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Most people are more honest than we assume
psychology.summary: How many people would lie to win a small bonus if nobody could catch them? Researchers in Norway pooled 11 online experiments, with over 8,000 answers, where people could secretly cheat for money. About 30% did. But people guessed far higher, overestimating cheating by about 14 percentage points. Managers guessed 55% would lie in one dice game.
psychology.why: Jareef Martuza, Helge Thorbjørnsen and Hallgeir Sjåstad published this in 2026. When managers learned the real honesty figures, they backed less workplace surveillance. Limits: every participant was a US online volunteer, and support for surveillance was measured as stated opinion, not real company decisions.
psychology.soWhat: Assuming everyone cheats can push offices and housing societies towards cameras, checks and rules that punish the honest majority.
psychology.take: Start with trust, and verify only where the stakes demand it.
psychology.watch: Count how many rules at your office assume staff will cheat.

terms.meaning: Plain difference between two percentages

sources.label: Martuza, Thorbjørnsen and Sjåstad (2026), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

study.authors: Jareef Martuza, Helge Thorbjørnsen and Hallgeir Sjåstad

psychology.example: A society secretary installs a lock on the shared bookshelf, sure that residents will steal books.
psychology.useThisWeek: Before adding a check or rule for others, ask what share would actually misbehave.

psychology.label: Psychology · 21 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Five minutes a day of small good deeds lifted mood
psychology.summary: Can a few minutes a day make you happier? In the Big Joy Project, people got one tiny task by email each day for a week: list things you're grateful for, do something kind, notice something awe-inspiring. Among 17,598 people from 169 countries, average emotional well-being rose from about 6.1 to 7.1 out of 10. Stress fell too.
psychology.why: Researchers led by Darwin Guevarra and Elissa Epel published it in 2025. People who did more tasks gained more, and those facing money strain gained most. The big limit: there was no comparison group, and volunteers were already keen on well-being.
psychology.soWhat: A cheap, short habit like a gratitude list costs nothing and may ease a stressful week.
psychology.take: Small daily kindnesses are underrated, but this study cannot prove they work.
psychology.watch: A randomised trial comparing these tasks with doing nothing, which the authors want.

terms.meaning: People who skip the treatment, for fair contrast

study.authors: Darwin A. Guevarra, Yoobin Park, Xuhai Xu, Jin Liou, Jolene Smith, Peggy Callahan, Emiliana Simon-Thomas and Elissa S. Epel

psychology.example: Writing three good things about your day on the metro ride home.
psychology.useThisWeek: Each evening for seven days, do one five-minute act: thank someone, help someone, or write a gratitude list.

marketing.label: India · 21 Nov 2026
marketing.headline: Google Gemini mocks a pushy, paywalled rival it simply invented
marketing.summary: Google has released three short films in India for Gemini, its AI assistant. Each one stars a made-up rival app called Chatty AI. In 'Date', 'Yoga' and 'Viva', Chatty AI keeps interrupting people with payment demands or locked features. Gemini then does the same job with free live video chat and unlimited free image uploads. Six social media creators play the users.
marketing.why: Comparison ads usually name a rival, which can invite complaints or legal fights. Inventing a fake competitor lets Google make the point safely. The films also show how people can bring their existing context into Gemini when they switch, removing a common reason to stay put.
marketing.soWhat: If you use a paid AI app, check Gemini's free tier first; for marketers, a fictional rival is a safe way to do comparison ads.
marketing.take: A made-up villain lets Google be cheeky without a legal fight.
marketing.watch: The three films running across Indian TV, cinema and social media feeds.

marketing.label: Global · 21 Nov 2026
marketing.headline: Bupa films real therapy sessions with Mary Berry and Freddie Flintoff
marketing.summary: Healthcare company Bupa has launched 'Mindplace Sessions', an unscripted YouTube series. Psychotherapist Owen O'Kane talks with baker Mary Berry, ex-cricketer Freddie Flintoff and broadcaster Miquita Oliver in three 30-minute episodes, plus a shorter one with Olly Bowman. They discuss grief, anxiety and shame. More than 100 short clips run on YouTube Shorts, TikTok, Instagram and LinkedIn.
marketing.why: Bupa surveyed 6,000 adults in the UK, Spain and Australia. About 83% said talking therapy could help, but only 8% get support. Nearly a quarter would consider it if they knew what happens in a session. Bupa also runs Mindplace therapy clinics, with about 70 open.
marketing.soWhat: If therapy feels scary, watching a real session can show you it is mostly a calm conversation.
marketing.take: Showing a whole session builds more trust than any 30-second mental-health ad.
